questions.question: A matrix has eigenvalues \(-1\) and \(-2\). The corresponding eigenvectors are \[\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}\] and \[\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}\] respectively. The matrix is
questions.explanation:
Given the eigenvectors \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) corresponding to the eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 = -1\) and \(\lambda_2 = -2\) respectively: \[X_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} \text{ for } \lambda_1 = -1, \qquad X_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} \text{ for } \lambda_2 = -2\] Let the unknown \(2 \times 2\) matrix \(A\) be defined as: \[A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}\] Case 1: For \(\lambda_1 = -1\) and \(X_1\)
\[\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} = (-1) \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}\] \[\begin{bmatrix} a - b \\ c - d \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\] \[a - b = -1 \qquad \text{--- (1)}\] \[c - d = 1 \qquad \text{--- (2)}\] Case 2: For \(\lambda_2 = -2\) and \(X_2\)
\[\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} = (-2) \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}\] \[\begin{bmatrix} a - 2b \\ c - 2d \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}\] \[a - 2b = -2 \qquad \text{--- (3)}\] \[c - 2d = 4 \qquad \text{--- (4)}\] Solving for \(a\) and \(b\):
Subtracting equation (3) from equation (1): \[(a - b) - (a - 2b) = -1 - (-2) \implies b = 1\] \[a - 1 = -1 \implies a = 0\] Solving for \(c\) and \(d\):
Subtracting equation (4) from equation (2): \[(c - d) - (c - 2d) = 1 - 4 \implies d = -3\] \[c - (-3) = 1 \implies c + 3 = 1 \implies c = -2\] \[A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -2 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\] \[\boxed{\text{(D) $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -2 & -3 \end{bmatrix}$}}\]

questions.question: A function \(y = 5x^2 + 10x\) is defined over an open interval \(x = (1, 2)\). At least at one point in this interval, \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) is exactly
questions.explanation:
Given the function: \[y = 5x^2 + 10x\] defined over the open interval \(x \in (1, 2)\). According to Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem (LMVT), if a function \(y = f(x)\) is continuous on a closed interval \([a, b]\) and differentiable on the open interval \((a, b)\), then there exists at least one point \(c \in (a, b)\) such that: \[f'(c) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}\] Here, the interval boundaries are \(a = 1\) and \(b = 2\). Let us calculate the value of the function at these boundary points:
  • At \(x = 1\): \[f(1) = 5(1)^2 + 10(1) = 5 + 10 = 15\]
  • At \(x = 2\): \[f(2) = 5(2)^2 + 10(2) = 5(4) + 20 = 20 + 20 = 40\]
Applying Mean Value Theorem, there must be at least one point in the interval \((1, 2)\) where the derivative \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) equals the average rate of change across the interval: \[\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{f(2) - f(1)}{2 - 1}\] \[\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{40 - 15}{1} = 25\] Hence, at least at one point in the given interval, \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) is exactly \(25\). Verification: Let's find the exact point \(x\) where this occurs by differentiating the function directly: \[\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{d}{dx}(5x^2 + 10x) = 10x + 10\] Equating the derivative to \(25\): \[10x + 10 = 25\] \[10x = 15 \implies x = 1.5\] Since \(x = 1.5\) lies perfectly inside the open interval \((1, 2)\), the theorem holds true. \[\boxed{\text{(b) } 25}\]

questions.question: Square roots of \(-i\), where \(i = \sqrt{-1}\) , are
questions.explanation: Let us assume: \[x = \sqrt{-i}\] In polar form, using the principal argument \(\theta = -\frac{\pi}{2}\): \[-i = \cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right) + i\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = e^{-i\frac{\pi}{2}}\] Taking the square root to find the first root (\(x_1\)): \[x = \left(e^{-i\frac{\pi}{2}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\] \[x = e^{-i\frac{\pi}{4}} = \cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right) + i\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\] Using \(\theta = \frac{3\pi}{2}\) to find the second root (\(x_2\)): \[-i = \cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}\right) + i\sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}\right) = e^{i\frac{3\pi}{2}}\] Taking the square root: \[x = \left(e^{i\frac{3\pi}{2}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} = e^{i\frac{3\pi}{4}}\] \[x = \cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}\right) + i\sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}\right)\] \[\boxed{B. \cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right) + i\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right), \ \cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}\right) + i\sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}\right)}\]

questions.question: \(\oint \frac{z^2 - 4}{z^2 + 4} \ dz\) evaluated anticlockwise around the circle \(|z - i| = 2\) , where \(i = \sqrt{-1}\) , is
questions.explanation:
The given contour integral is: \[\oint_{C} \frac{z^2 - 4}{z^2 + 4} \, dz \quad \text{where} \quad C: |z - i| = 2\] \[f(z) = \frac{z^2 - 4}{(z - 2i)(z + 2i)}\] The singularities of \(f(z)\) are simple poles at: \[z = 2i \quad \text{and} \quad z = -2i\] The given contour \(C\) is a circle centered at \(i\) (or \((0,1)\) in the Cartesian plane) with a radius of \(2\). Let us test which poles lie inside this contour:
  • For \(z = 2i\): \[|2i - i| = |i| = 1 < 2 \implies z = 2i \text{ lies inside the curve } C.\]
  • For \(z = -2i\): \[|-2i - i| = |-3i| = 3 > 2 \implies z = -2i \text{ lies outside the curve } C.\]
By Cauchy's Residue Theorem, the value of the integral depends only on the residue of the pole inside the contour: \[\oint_{C} \frac{z^2 - 4}{z^2 + 4} \, dz = 2\pi i \, \text{Res}\{f(z), 2i\}\] Finding the residue at the simple pole \(z = 2i\): \[\text{Res}\{f(z), 2i\} = \lim_{z \to 2i} (z - 2i) \frac{z^2 - 4}{(z - 2i)(z + 2i)} = \frac{(2i)^2 - 4}{2i + 2i}\] \[\text{Res}\{f(z), 2i\} = \frac{4i^2 - 4}{4i}\] \[\text{Res}\{f(z), 2i\} = \frac{-4 - 4}{4i} = \frac{-8}{4i} = -\frac{2}{i}\] Therefore, \[\oint_{C} \frac{z^2 - 4}{z^2 + 4} \, dz = 2\pi i \left( -\frac{2}{i} \right) = -4\pi\] \[\boxed{A. -4\pi}\]

questions.question: A continuous random variable \(X\) has a probability density function \[f(x)=e^{-x}, \quad 0<x<\infty.\] Then \(P\{X>1\}\) is
questions.explanation: Given probability density function: \[f(x)=e^{-x}, \qquad 0<x<\infty\] We need to find \[P(X>1)\] Using the definition of probability for a continuous random variable, \[P(X>1)=\int_{1}^{\infty} e^{-x}\,dx\] Evaluating, \[P(X>1)=\left[-e^{-x}\right]_{1}^{\infty}\] \[P(X>1)=0-(-e^{-1})\] \[P(X>1)=\frac{1}{e}\approx 0.368\] \[\boxed{\text{(a) }0.368}\]

questions.question: Consider a delta connection of resistors and its equivalent star connection as shown below. If all elements of the delta connection are scaled by a factor \(k\), \(k>0\), the element of the corresponding star equivalent will be scaled by a factor of
questions.explanation: For a delta-to-star transformation, \[R_A = \frac{R_bR_c} {R_a+R_b+R_c}, \quad R_B = \frac{R_cR_a} {R_a+R_b+R_c}, \quad R_C = \frac{R_aR_b} {R_a+R_b+R_c}\] If all delta resistances are scaled by a factor \(k\), \[R_a'=kR_a, \qquad R_b'=kR_b, \qquad R_c'=kR_c\] Then, \[R_A' = \frac{R_b'R_c'} {R_a'+R_b'+R_c'} = \frac{(kR_b)(kR_c)} {k(R_a+R_b+R_c)}\] \[R_A' = k\frac{R_bR_c} {R_a+R_b+R_c} = kR_A\] Similarly, \[R_B'=kR_B, \qquad R_C'=kR_C\] Therefore, \[\boxed{\textbf{B. }k}\]

questions.question: Two magnetically uncoupled inductive coils have Q factors \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) at the chosen operating frequency. Their respective resistances are \(R_1\) and \(R_2\). When connected in series, their effective Q factor at the same operating frequency is
questions.explanation:
For Coil 1, the quality factor is given by: \[q_{1} = \frac{\omega L_{1}}{R_{1}}\] Rearranging for the self-inductance of Coil 1: \[L_{1} = \frac{q_{1} R_{1}}{\omega}\] Similarly, for Coil 2, the quality factor is: \[q_{2} = \frac{\omega L_{2}}{R_{2}}\] Rearranging for the self-inductance of Coil 2: \[L_{2} = \frac{q_{2} R_{2}}{\omega}\] When the two coils are connected in series, the equivalent parameters are:
  • Equivalent inductance: \(L_{eq} = L_{1} + L_{2}\)
  • Equivalent resistance: \(R_{eq} = R_{1} + R_{2}\)
The overall quality factor \(Q\) of the series combination is defined as: \[Q = \frac{\omega (L_{1} + L_{2})}{R_{1} + R_{2}}\] Substituting the expressions for \(L_{1}\) and \(L_{2}\) into the equation: \[Q = \frac{\omega \left[ \dfrac{q_{1} R_{1}}{\omega} + \dfrac{q_{2} R_{2}}{\omega} \right]}{R_{1} + R_{2}}\] Simplifying the expression by cancelling \(\omega\): \[\boxed{Q = \frac{q_{1} R_{1} + q_{2} R_{2}}{R_{1} + R_{2}}}\] \[\boxed{(c) (q_1R_1+q_2R_2)/(R_1+R_2)}\]

questions.question: A single-phase load is supplied by a single-phase voltage source. If the current flowing from the load to the source is \(10\angle-150^{\circ}\) A and if the voltage at the load terminals is \(100\angle60^{\circ}\), then the
options: load absorbs real power and delivers reactive power.
load absorbs real power and absorbs reactive power.
load delivers real power and delivers reactive power.
load delivers real power and absorbs reactive power.
questions.explanation: We know that complex power S is given by : \[S=VI^*\] Here \(V=100\angle60^{\circ}V\) and \(I=10\angle-150^{\circ}A\). Therefore complex power \(S=100\angle60^{\circ}\times 10\angle150^{\circ}=1000\angle210^{\circ}\,\text{VA}\) Now, \(S=P+jQ\) Thus, \(1000\angle210^{\circ}=1000\cos210^{\circ}+j1000\sin210^{\circ}\) From this we can conclude, \(P=1000\cos210^{\circ}=-866.025\,\text{W}\) and \(Q=1000\sin210^{\circ}=-500 \,\text{VAR}\) According to convention when current flows from load to source when the terminal where current enters load is taken as positive, power > 0 indicates power is absorbed by load and power < 0 indicates power is delivered by load. Here current flows from load to source. Since only one of the conditions is altered, the criteria to determine whether power is absorbed or delivered is reversed, i.e.,here power < 0 indicates power is absorbed by load and power > 0 indicates power is delivered by load. Since both active and reactive powers are negative, both active and reactive powers are absorbed by load. \[\boxed{(b) \textit{load absorbs real power and absorbs reactive power.}}\]

questions.explanation: According to maximum power transfer theorem, the purely resistive load should have a value equal to the magnitude of the internal impedance of the source in order to have maximum power transferred to it. \[R_L = |Z_{in}|\implies R_L = \sqrt{4^2+3^2}=5\Omega\] \[\boxed{(c) 5}\]

questions.question: The impulse response of a continuous time system is given by \[h(t)=\delta(t-1)+\delta(t-3).\] The value of the step response at \(t=2\) is
questions.explanation: The step response of an LTI system is the response to the unit step input: \[s(t)=h(t)*u(t).\] Given, \[h(t)=\delta(t-1)+\delta(t-3).\] Using the property \[\delta(t-a)*u(t)=u(t-a),\] the step response is \[s(t)=u(t-1)+u(t-3).\] At \(t=2\), \[s(2)=u(1)+u(-1)=1+0=1.\] \[\boxed{\text{(b) }1}\]

questions.question: Two systems with impulse responses \(h_{1}(t)\) and \(h_{2}(t)\) are connected in cascade. Then the overall impulse response of the cascade system is given by
questions.explanation:
For two LTI systems connected in cascade, the overall impulse response is obtained by convolving the individual impulse responses. Let the impulse responses be \(h_{1}(t)\) and \(h_{2}(t)\). The overall impulse response is \[h(t)=h_{1}(t)*h_{2}(t)
=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}h_{1}(\tau)\,h_{2}(t-\tau)\,d\tau.\] Hence, the cascade connection is represented by the convolution of the two impulse responses. \[\boxed{\text{(c) Convolution of }h_{1}(t)\text{ and }h_{2}(t)}\]

questions.question: For a periodic signal \[v(t)=30\sin 100t+10\cos 300t+6\sin\left(500t+\frac{\pi}{4}\right),\] the fundamental frequency in \(\mathrm{rad/s}\) is
questions.explanation:
Given, \[v(t)=30\sin(100t)+10\cos(300t)+6\sin\left(500t+\frac{\pi}{4}\right).\] The angular frequencies present in the signal are \[100,\;300,\;500\ \text{rad/s}.\] The fundamental angular frequency is the greatest common divisor (GCD) of all component frequencies: \[\omega_0=\gcd(100,300,500)=100\ \text{rad/s}.\] The given signal can therefore be written as \[v(t)=30\sin(\omega_0t)
+10\cos(3\omega_0t)
+6\sin\left(5\omega_0t+\frac{\pi}{4}\right),\] showing that all components are harmonics of \(100\,\text{rad/s}\). \[\boxed{\text{(a) }100\ \text{rad/s}}\]

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: A band-limited signal with a maximum frequency of \(5~\mathrm{kHz}\) is to be sampled. According to the sampling theorem, the sampling frequency in \(\mathrm{kHz}\) which is not valid is
questions.explanation:
A band-limited signal has the maximum frequency \[f_{\max}=5\,\text{kHz}.\] According to the Nyquist sampling theorem, the minimum sampling frequency is \[f_{s}\geq 2f_{\max}=2\times5=10\,\text{kHz}.\] Check each option against the Nyquist criterion: \[\begin{aligned}
5\,\text{kHz} &< 10\,\text{kHz}\quad\text{(Not valid)},\\
12\,\text{kHz} &> 10\,\text{kHz}\quad\text{(Valid)},\\
15\,\text{kHz} &> 10\,\text{kHz}\quad\text{(Valid)},\\
20\,\text{kHz} &> 10\,\text{kHz}\quad\text{(Valid)}.
\end{aligned}\] Hence, the only invalid sampling frequency is \(5\,\text{kHz}\). \[\boxed{\text{(a) }5\,\text{kHz}}\]

questions.question: Which one of the following statements is NOT TRUE for a continuous time causal and stable LTI system?
options: All the poles of the system must lie on the left side of the \(j\omega\) axis.
Zeros of the system can lie anywhere in the \(s\)-plane.
All the poles must lie within \(|s|=1\).
All the roots of the characteristic equation must be located on the left side of the \(j\omega\) axis.
questions.explanation:
For a continuous-time LTI system to be causal and BIBO stable,
  • All poles must lie in the left half of the \(s\)-plane, i.e., \[\Re(s)<0.\] Hence, statements A and D are true.
  • System zeros do not affect stability and may lie anywhere in the \(s\)-plane. Hence, statement B is true.
  • Statement C is false because stability requires poles to satisfy \[\Re(s)<0,\] not \[|s|<1.\] For example, a pole at \(s=-2\) is stable but lies outside the circle \(|s|=1\).
\[\boxed{\text{(c) All the poles must lie within }|s|=1}\]

questions.question: The impulse response of a system is \[h(t)=tu(t).\] For an input \(u(t-1)\), the output is
questions.explanation: Using Laplace transforms, \[H(s)=\mathcal{L}\{tu(t)\}=\frac{1}{s^2},\] and \[X(s)=\mathcal{L}\{u(t-1)\}=\frac{e^{-s}}{s}.\] Therefore, \[Y(s)=H(s)X(s)=\frac{e^{-s}}{s^3}.\] Taking the inverse Laplace transform, \[y(t)=\frac{(t-1)^2}{2}\,u(t-1).\] \[\boxed{\text{(c) }\dfrac{(t-1)^2}{2}\,u(t-1)}\]

questions.question: In the circuit shown below, the knee current of the ideal Zener diode is \(10\text{mA}\). To maintain \(5\text{ V}\) across \(R_L\), the minimum value of \(R_L\) in \(\Omega\) and the minimum power rating of the Zener diode in \(\text{mW}\) respectively are
questions.explanation: The minimum Zener current required for regulation is \[I_{Z(\min)}=I_{Z(\text{knee})}=10~\text{mA}\] The current through the \(100~\Omega\) resistor is \[I = \frac{10-5}{100} = 50~\text{mA}\] Applying KCL, \(I=I_Z+I_L\) For the minimum value of \(R_L\), the load current is maximum while the Zener current is at its knee value. Hence, \[I_{L(\max)} = 50-10 = 40~\text{mA}\] Therefore, \[R_{L(\min)} = \frac{V_Z}{I_{L(\max)}} = \frac{5}{40\times10^{-3}} = 125~\Omega\] The maximum Zener current occurs when the load is open-circuited. \[I_{Z(\max)}=50~\text{mA}\] Hence, the maximum power dissipated in the Zener diode is \[P_{Z(\max)} = V_ZI_{Z(\max)} = 5\times50~\text{mA} = 250~\text{mW}\] Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{B. }125\ and \ 250}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: In the circuit shown below what is the output voltage (\(V_{\text{out}}\)) in Volts if a silicon transistor Q and an ideal op-amp are used?
questions.explanation:
Case 1: Assume \(Q\) is OFF (Cutoff)
  • With \(Q\) cutoff, no feedback exists to the op-amp.
  • The op-amp acts as an open-loop comparator: \[V_- = 5\,\text{V}, \quad V_+ = 0\,\text{V}\]
  • Since \(V_- > V_+\), output saturates at negative supply: \[V_{\text{out}} = -15\,\text{V}\]
  • For transistor \(Q\), base potential \(V_B = 0\,\text{V}\) and emitter potential \(V_E = V_{\text{out}} = -15\,\text{V}\).
  • This gives \(V_{BE} = V_B - V_E = 0 - (-15) = +15\,\text{V} > 0.7\,\text{V}\), which forward biases the base-emitter junction.
  • Contradiction! Hence, \(Q\) cannot be in cutoff.
Case 2: Transistor \(Q\) is Active / ON
  • With \(Q\) conducting, negative feedback path is established.
  • Virtual ground concept holds at the inverting terminal: \[V_- = V_+ = 0\,\text{V}\]
  • Collector terminal potential \(V_C = V_- = 0\,\text{V}\).
  • Base terminal is directly grounded: \[V_B = 0\,\text{V}\]
  • Since \(V_{BE} = V_B - V_E = 0.7\,\text{V}\) for a silicon transistor: \[V_E = V_B - 0.7\,\text{V} = 0 - 0.7\,\text{V} = -0.7\,\text{V}\]
  • Since the output \(V_{\text{out}}\) is connected directly to the emitter of \(Q\): \[V_{\text{out}} = -0.7\,\text{V}\]
\[\boxed{(B) \ \ -0.7}\]
Mistakes to avoid
Do not assume the op-amp is simply saturated without checking whether the feedback transistor turns ON.

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: In the circuit shown below the op-amps are ideal. Then \(V_{\text{out}}\) in Volts is
questions.explanation: Since no current enters the ideal op-amp inputs, non-inverting terminal voltage of first stage: \[V_+ = +1\,\text{V}\] By virtual short concept, \(V_- = V_+ = +1\,\text{V}\). Nodal analysis at the inverting node \(V_-\): \[\frac{1 - (-2)}{1\,\text{k}\Omega} + \frac{1 - V}{1\,\text{k}\Omega} = 0\] \[3 + 1 - V = 0 \implies V = 4\,\text{V}\] The second stage acts as a non-inverting amplifier with gain: \[A_v = 1 + \frac{R_f}{R_1} = 1 + \frac{1\,\text{k}\Omega}{1\,\text{k}\Omega} = 2\] Therefore, the final output voltage: \[V_{\text{out}} = V \times 2= 4 \times 2 = 8\,\text{V}\] \[\boxed{(C) \ \ 8}\]

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.ref: Logic Gates and Boolean Algebra Q1
questions.question: A bulb in a staircase has two switches, one switch being at the ground floor and the other one at the first floor. The bulb can be turned ON and also can be turned OFF by any one of the switches irrespective of the state of the other switch. The logic of switching of the bulb resembles
questions.explanation:
Let the two staircase switches be represented by inputs \(A\) and \(B\). The bulb should change its state whenever any one of the switches is toggled, irrespective of the state of the other switch. The bulb is ON when the switches are in opposite positions and OFF when the switches are in the same position. The truth table is \[\begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline A & B & \text{Bulb} \\ \hline 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \hline 0 & 1 & 1 \\ \hline 1 & 0 & 1 \\ \hline 1 & 1 & 0 \\ \hline \end{array}\] The above truth table corresponds to the Exclusive-OR (XOR) gate. Therefore, \[\text{Bulb} = A \oplus B\] (C) An XOR gate
Key points
  • An XOR gate produces HIGH output when its inputs are different.
  • The Boolean expression of XOR is \[A \oplus B = \overline{A}B + A\overline{B}.\]
  • In staircase wiring, toggling either switch changes the state of the bulb, which is the characteristic behavior of an XOR gate.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse staircase switching with an OR gate. In an OR gate, the output remains HIGH when both inputs are HIGH, whereas the bulb is OFF when both switches are in the same position.
  • Remember that XOR gives HIGH only when the inputs are unequal.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: The clock frequency applied to the digital circuit shown in figure below is 1,kHz. If the initial state of the output \(Q\) of the flip-flop is `0', then the frequency of the output waveform \(Q\) in kHz is
questions.explanation:
Given: Clock frequency \(f_{\text{in}} = 1\,\text{kHz}\), and initial state \(Q = 0\). 1. Derivation of Combinational Logic Expression:
To determine the input to the \(T\) flip-flop (\(T = X\)), we analyze the logic gates step-by-step using the complementary outputs \(Q\) and \(\bar{Q}\):
  • XOR Gate Output: The inputs are \(Q\) and \(\bar{Q}\). Since one input is always the complement of the other, the output is: \[Y_1 = Q \oplus \bar{Q} = 1\]
  • XNOR Gate Output: The inputs are also \(Q\) and \(\bar{Q}\). Since the inputs are always different, the output is: \[Y_2 = Q \odot \bar{Q} = 0\]
  • NAND Gate Output (\(X\)): The inputs to the NAND gate are the outputs of the XOR and XNOR gates (\(Y_1\) and \(Y_2\)): \[X = \overline{Y_1 \cdot Y_2} = \overline{1 \cdot 0} = \overline{0} = 1\]
Since \(T = X\), the flip-flop input is permanently held at: \[T = 1\] This proves that the \(T\) flip-flop operates strictly in toggle mode for all clock events. 2. State Transition Table:
Using \(T = 1\), we trace the state transition sequence: The output sequence alternates indefinitely as: \[0 \rightarrow 1 \rightarrow 0 \rightarrow 1 \rightarrow \dots\] Thus, the total number of distinct states in the repeating cycle is: \[M = 2\] This confirms that the circuit behaves as a MOD-2 counter (or a divide-by-2 frequency divider). 3. Output Frequency Calculation:
The frequency of the output waveform \(Q\) is given by: \[f_{\text{out}} = \frac{f_{\text{in}}}{M} = \frac{1\,\text{kHz}}{2} = 0.5\,\text{kHz}\] Hence, the correct option is (B). (B) 0.5
Key points
  • A \(T\) flip-flop with its input tied to a permanent high logic level (\(T = 1\)) remains constantly in toggle mode.
  • Any sequential network forming a stable loop of 2 states acts as a MOD-2 counter, cutting the driving input clock frequency exactly in half (\(f_{\text{out}} = f_{\text{clk}}/2\)).

questions.question: In the circuit shown below, \(Q_1\) has negligible collector-to-emitter saturation voltage and the diode drops negligible voltage across it under forward bias. If \(V_{CC} = +5\,\text{V}\), \(X\) and \(Y\) are digital signals with \(0\,\text{V}\) as logic 0 and \(V_{CC}\) as logic 1, then the Boolean expression for \(Z\) is
questions.explanation:
Given circuit is shown below, Here, transistor (\(Q_1\)) and diode (\(D\)) both can work as a switch and transistor (\(Q_1\)) is controlled by input (\(X\)) and diode (\(D\)) is controlled by input (\(Y\)). Condition 1 : When \(X = 0\) and \(Y = 0\). Transistor \(Q_1\) is operated under cutoff mode, it means open circuited (OFF) and diode \(D\) is in forward bias mode, it means short circuited (ON). Hence, \(X = 0\) and \(Y = 0 \rightarrow Z = V_{\text{out}} = 0\) (because of short circuit) Condition 2 : When \(X = 0\) and \(Y = 1\). Transistor \(Q_1\) is operated under cutoff mode, it means open circuited (OFF) and diode \(D\) is in reverse bias mode, it means open circuited (OFF). Hence, \(X = 0\) and \(Y = 1 \rightarrow Z = V_{\text{out}} = +V_{cc} = 1\) (because of open circuit) Condition 3 : When \(X = 1\) and \(Y = 0\). Transistor \(Q_1\) is operated under saturation mode, it means short circuited (ON) and diode \(D\) is in forward bias mode, it means short circuited (ON). Hence, \(X = 1\) and \(Y = 0 \rightarrow Z = V_{\text{out}} = 0\) (because of short circuit) Condition 4 : When \(X = 1\) and \(Y = 1\). Transistor \(Q_1\) is operated under saturation mode, it means short circuited (ON) and diode \(D\) is in reverse bias mode, it means open circuited (OFF). Hence, \(X = 1\) and \(Y = 1 \rightarrow Z = V_{\text{out}} = 0\) (because of short circuit) Based on above four condition we can form truth table as, \[\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \multicolumn{2}{|c|}{\textbf{Input}} & \textbf{Transistor} & \textbf{Diode} & \textbf{Output} \\ \hline X & Y & Q & D & Z \\ \hline 0 & 0 & \text{OFF} & \text{ON} & 0 \\ \hline 0 & 1 & \text{OFF} & \text{OFF} & 1 \\ \hline 1 & 0 & \text{ON} & \text{ON} & 0 \\ \hline 1 & 1 & \text{ON} & \text{OFF} & 0 \\ \hline \end{array}\] K-map of function \(Z\) in SOP form is, Thus, \(Z = \overline{X}Y\) (B) \(\bar{X}Y\)
Key points
  • A transistor under cutoff is an open circuit (OFF); under saturation it is a short circuit (ON).
  • A diode in forward bias is a short circuit; in reverse bias it is an open circuit.
  • Wired-AND at the common interconnecting node: \(Z = \bar{X} \cdot Y\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • The diode is controlled by \(Y\) directly (not \(\bar{Y}\)): when \(Y = 1\), diode is reverse biased (OFF); when \(Y = 0\), diode is forward biased (ON). Do not confuse the bias direction.

questions.question: The signal flow graph for a system is given below. The transfer function \(\dfrac{Y(s)}{U(s)}\) for this system is
questions.explanation:
Using Mason’s gain formulae:
  • Forward Paths: \(P_{1} = s^{-2} = \dfrac{1}{s^2}\) and \(P_{2} = s^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{s}\)
  • Feedback Loops: \(L_{1} = -2s^{-1}\), \(L_{2} = -2s^{-2}\), \(L_{3} = -4\), \(L_{4} = -4s^{-1}\)
  • System Determinant (\(\Delta\)): \[\Delta = 1 - [-2s^{-1} - 2s^{-2} - 4 - 4s^{-1}]\] \[\Delta = 1 + \frac{2}{s} + \frac{2}{s^2} + 4 + \frac{4}{s} = \frac{5s^2 + 6s + 2}{s^2}\]
  • Path Cofactors: \(\Delta_{1} = 1\), \(\Delta_{2} = 1\)
Applying the transfer function formula: \[\frac{Y(s)}{U(s)} = \frac{\sum P_{k}\Delta_{k}}{\Delta} = \frac{\dfrac{1}{s^2} \times 1 + \dfrac{1}{s} \times 1}{\dfrac{5s^2 + 6s + 2}{s^2}} =\frac{s + 1}{5s^2 + 6s + 2}\] \[\boxed{(A) \ \ \dfrac{s + 1}{5s^2 + 6s + 2}}\]

questions.question: The open-loop transfer function of a dc motor is given as \(\dfrac{\omega(s)}{V_a (s)} = \dfrac{10}{1+10 s}\). When connected in feedback as shown below, the approximate value of \(K_a\) that will reduce the time constant of the closed loop system by one hundred times as compared to that of the open-loop system is
questions.explanation:
Given the open-loop transfer function of a dc motor: \[\frac{\omega(s)}{V_a(s)} = \frac{10}{1 + 10s} = \frac{10}{1 + \tau s}\] \[\tau = 10\] The closed-loop transfer function is given by: \[\frac{\omega(s)}{R(s)} = \frac{G(s)}{1 + G(s)H(s)} = \frac{\dfrac{10K_a}{1 + 10s}}{1 + \dfrac{10K_a}{1 + 10s}} = \frac{10K_a}{1 + 10K_a + 10s}\] To find the closed-loop time constant, we rearrange the denominator into the standard form \((1 + \tau_{cl}s)\): \[\frac{\omega(s)}{R(s)} = \frac{\dfrac{10K_a}{1 + 10K_a}}{1 + \left(\dfrac{10}{1 + 10K_a}\right)s} \implies \quad \tau_{cl} = \frac{10}{1 + 10K_a}\] According to the problem statement, the closed-loop time constant is reduced by one hundred times compared to the open-loop time constant: \[\tau_{cl} = \frac{\tau}{100}\] \[\frac{10}{1 + 10K_a} = \frac{1}{100} \times 10\] \[K_a = 9.9 \approx 10\] \[\boxed{(C) \ \ 10}\]
Key points
  • The standard form of a first-order system transfer function is \(\dfrac{K}{1 + \tau s}\), where \(\tau\) represents the time constant.
  • Negative feedback reduces the time constant of a system by a factor of \((1 + GH)\), thereby increasing the speed of response (bandwidth).
Mistakes to avoid
Incorrect Time Constant Extraction: Do not mistake the coefficient of \(s\) as the time constant before ensuring the constant term in the denominator is normalized to \(1\). Always bring the expression to the form \(1 + \tau s\).

questions.question: The separately excited dc motor in the figure below has a rated armature current of 20 A and a rated armature voltage of 150 V. An ideal chopper switching at 5 kHz is used to control the armature voltage. If \(L_a= 0.1\text{ mH}\), \(R_a= 1\ \Omega\), neglecting armature reaction, the duty ratio of the chopper to obtain 50% of the rated torque at the rated speed and the rated field current is . [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
The armature loop equation for a DC motor under steady-state operating conditions is defined as: \[V_{a} = E_{b} + I_{a} R_{a}\] Initially, substituting the known operating parameter values (\(V_{a} = 150\,\text{V}\), \(I_{a} = 20\,\text{A}\), and \(R_{a} = 1\,\Omega\)) into the voltage relation: \[150 = E_{b} + 20 \times 1\] \[E_{b} = 130\,\text{V}\] Since the electromagnetic torque developed by a DC motor is directly proportional to its armature current (\(T \propto I_{a}\)) under constant field flux conditions, operating at half the rated torque reduces the required current by half: \[I_{a} = 10\,\text{A}\] The newly required terminal voltage \(V_{a}\) to sustain operation at this torque level while keeping the speed (and hence the back EMF, \(E_{b}\)) constant is: \[V_{a} = 130 + 10 \times 1 = 140\,\text{V}\] Assuming a chopping circuit configures the variable voltage supply with a total source potential of \(200\,\text{V}\), the required duty cycle \(D\) is calculated as: \[D = \frac{140}{200} = 0.7\] Therefore, the duty cycle of the converter is: \[\boxed{(D)\, 0.7}\]
Key points
  • DC Motor Voltage Equation: The applied terminal voltage matches the sum of the internally generated back EMF and the internal resistance voltage drop (\(V_{a} = E_{b} + I_{a}R_{a}\)).
  • Torque-Current Dependency: Under constant field excitation, the developed mechanical torque varies directly with the current magnitude flowing through the armature (\(T \propto I_{a}\)).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Make sure not to change the back EMF value \(E_{b}\) unless a change in operating speed or magnetic flux is explicitly specified in the problem statement.

questions.question: A firm is selling its product at Rs. 60 per unit. The total cost of production is Rs. 100 and firm is earning total profit of Rs. 500. Later, the total cost increased by 30%. By what percentage the price should be increased to maintained the same profit level.
questions.explanation:
Let the number of units sold be \(n\). Initial State: \[\begin{aligned} \text{Total Revenue} &= 60n \\ \text{Total Cost} &= 100 \\ \text{Profit} &= \text{Total Revenue} - \text{Total Cost} = 500 \end{aligned}\] \[60n - 100 = 500 \implies 60n = 600 \implies n = 10 \text{ units}\] Modified State: The total cost increases by \(30\%\): \[\text{New Total Cost} = 100 \times 1.30 = 130\] To maintain the same profit of Rs. 500 with \(n = 10\) units, let the new selling price per unit be \(SP'\): \[10 \cdot SP' - 130 = 500 \implies 10 \cdot SP' = 630 \implies SP' = 63\] Percentage increase in selling price per unit: \[\text{Increase} = \frac{63 - 60}{60} \times 100 = \frac{3}{60} \times 100 = 5\%\] \[\boxed{\text{A: 5 }}\]
Key points
  • Profit Architecture: Profit is calculated globally as Total Revenue minus Total Cost, meaning percentage changes in total cost affect the aggregate equation linearly.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not apply the 30% cost increase directly as a 30% required price increase; prices must be calculated dynamically based on the fixed profit margin.

questions.question: If \(3 \leq X \leq 5\) and \(8 \leq Y \leq 11\) then which of the following options is TRUE?
questions.explanation:
Given the inequalities: \[3 \le X \le 5 \quad \text{and} \quad 8 \le Y \le 11\] To find the range of the fraction \(\frac{X}{Y}\), we determine its minimum and maximum possible values.
  • Minimum value: Occurs when the numerator is minimized and the denominator is maximized. \[\left(\frac{X}{Y}\right)_{\text{min}} = \frac{X_{\text{min}}}{Y_{\text{max}}} = \frac{3}{11}\]
  • Maximum value: Occurs when the numerator is maximized and the denominator is minimized. \[\left(\frac{X}{Y}\right)_{\text{max}} = \frac{X_{\text{max}}}{Y_{\text{min}}} = \frac{5}{8}\]
Combining these bounds gives: \[\frac{3}{11} \le \frac{X}{Y} \le \frac{5}{8}\] \[\boxed{\text{B: $\dfrac{3}{11} \le \dfrac{X}{Y} \le \dfrac{5}{8}$}}\]
Key points
  • Fraction Extremes: For positive intervals, a fraction \(\frac{A}{B}\) reaches its absolute minimum at \(\frac{A_{\text{min}}}{B_{\text{max}}}\) and its absolute maximum at \(\frac{A_{\text{max}}}{B_{\text{min}}}\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not simply divide the lower bounds together (\(\frac{3}{8}\)) or upper bounds together (\(\frac{5}{11}\)) to construct the range.

questions.question: Velocity of an object fired directly in upward direction is given by \(V = 80 - 32t\), where \(t\) (time) is in seconds. When will the velocity be between 32 m/sec and 64 m/sec?
questions.explanation:
The velocity equation is given as: \[V = 80 - 32t\] We want to find the time interval \(t\) during which the velocity is strictly between \(32\,\text{m/sec}\) and \(64\,\text{m/sec}\): \[32 < 80 - 32t < 64\] Subtract 80 from all parts of the inequality: \[32 - 80 < -32t < 64 - 80\] \[-48 < -32t < -16\] Divide by \(-32\). Remember that dividing an inequality by a negative number reverses the direction of the inequality signs: \[\frac{-48}{-32} > t > \frac{-16}{-32}\] \[\frac{3}{2} > t > \frac{1}{2} \implies t \in \left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{3}{2}\right)\] \[\boxed{\text{C: (1/2, 3/2) }}\]
Key points
  • Inequality Inversion: Multiplying or dividing an inequality by any negative value flips the inequality signs (\(<\) becomes \(>\)).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: In a factory, two machines M1 and M2 manufacture 60% and 40% of the autocomponents respectively. Out of the total production, 2% of M1 and 3% of M2 are found to be defective. If a randomly drawn autocomponent from the combined lot is found defective, what is the probability that it was manufactured by M2?
questions.explanation:
This problem can be modeled using Bayes' Theorem. Let:
  • \(M_1, M_2\) be the events that an autocomponent is manufactured by machine 1 and 2 respectively.
  • \(P(M_1) = 0.60\) and \(P(M_2) = 0.40\).
  • \(D\) be the event that a component is defective.
  • \(P(D|M_1) = 0.02\) and \(P(D|M_2) = 0.03\).
We need to find the conditional probability \(P(M_2|D)\): \[P(M_2|D) = \frac{P(M_2) \cdot P(D|M_2)}{P(M_1) \cdot P(D|M_1) + P(M_2) \cdot P(D|M_2)}\] Substitute the given values into the equation: \[\begin{aligned} P(M_2|D) &= \frac{0.40 \times 0.03}{(0.60 \times 0.02) + (0.40 \times 0.03)} \\ &= \frac{0.012}{0.012 + 0.012} \\ &= \frac{0.012}{0.024} = 0.5 \end{aligned}\] Wait, checking calculations: \(0.40 \times 0.03 = 0.012\). \(0.60 \times 0.02 = 0.012\). Total = 0.024. \(0.012/0.024 = 0.5\). \[\boxed{\text{C: 0.5}}\]
Key points
  • Bayes' Theorem: Evaluates the posterior probability of a specific cause given an observed event by dividing the probability of that specific pathway by the total probability across all pathways.

questions.question: If \(|-2X + 9| = 3\) then the possible value of \(|-X| - X^2\) would be:
questions.explanation:
Given the absolute value equation: \[|-2x + 9| = 3\] Since \(|-A| = |A|\), we can simplify this to: \[|2x - 9| = 3\] This splits into two cases: Case 1: \(2x - 9 = 3 \implies 2x = 12 \implies x = 6\). Case 2: \(2x - 9 = -3 \implies 2x = 6 \implies x = 3\). Now substitute these possible values of \(x\) into the objective expression \(|-x| - x^2 = x - x^2\) (since \(x\) values are positive):
  • For \(x = 6\): \(6 - 6^2 = 6 - 36 = -30\).
  • For \(x = 3\): \(3 - 3^2 = 3 - 9 = -6\).
Checking the options (30, -30, -42, 42), the value \(-30\) matches option B. \[\boxed{\text{B: -30}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Remember the final term is \(-x^2\), meaning you subtract the square of \(x\). A sign error here might lead to a false positive value like \(+30\).

questions.question: What will be the maximum sum of \(44, 42, 40, \dots\)?
questions.explanation:
The given sequence is an arithmetic progression (AP): \(44, 42, 40, \dots\) with a common difference \(d = -2\). To achieve the maximum sum, we must add all positive terms in the sequence and exclude any negative terms, as adding negative numbers reduces the total sum. Step 1: Identify the last positive term
Set the \(n^{\text{th}}\) term \(a_n > 0\): \[a_n = a + (n-1)d > 0\] \[44 + (n-1)(-2) > 0 \implies 44 - 2n + 2 > 0\] \[46 > 2n \implies n < 23\] Since \(n\) must be an integer, the last positive term is the \(22^{\text{nd}}\) term: \[a_{22} = 44 + (22-1)(-2) = 44 - 42 = 2\] Step 2: Calculate the sum of these 22 terms
Using the AP sum formula \(S_n = \frac{n}{2}(a + l)\): \[S_{22} = \frac{22}{2}(44 + 2) = 11 \times 46 = 506\] \[\boxed{\text{C: 506}}\]
Key points
  • Maximum Sum of a Decreasing AP: Always bounded by accumulating all non-negative terms (\(a_n \ge 0\)).

questions.question: Out of all the 2-digit integers between 1 and 100, a 2-digit number has to be selected at random. What is the probability that the selected number is not divisible by 7?
questions.explanation:
To find the probability that a randomly selected 2-digit number is not divisible by 7, we evaluate the complementary probability of the numbers that are divisible by 7. Step 1: Identify the total sample space
The 2-digit integers range strictly from \(10\) to \(99\). \[\text{Total 2-digit integers} = 99 - 10 + 1 = 90\] Step 2: Count 2-digit integers divisible by 7
The multiples of 7 within this specific range are \(14, 21, 28, \dots, 98\). This forms an Arithmetic Progression (AP) where the first term \(a = 14\), the common difference \(d = 7\), and the last term \(l = 98\). Using the standard AP formula \(l = a + (n-1)d\): \[\begin{aligned} 98 &= 14 + (n-1)7 \\ 84 &= 7(n-1) \\ n - 1 &= 12 \implies n = 13 \end{aligned}\] There are exactly 13 two-digit integers that are divisible by 7. Step 3: Calculate the complementary probability
The number of 2-digit integers not divisible by 7 is the complement of our subset: \[\text{Count} = 90 - 13 = 77\] \[P(\text{Not Divisible}) = \frac{77}{90}\] \[\boxed{\text{D: 77/90}}\]
Key points
  • Complementary Probability: Calculating the probability of an event's complement (\(1 - P(A)\)) is often much simpler than counting the valid outcomes directly.
  • Legacy Key Note: Based on standard technical corrections to this legacy GATE question, option D is the absolute mathematical assignment.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Sample Space Error: Do not calculate the total number of 2-digit integers as \(99 - 10 = 89\). Remember to add 1 to include both boundary extremes in an inclusive interval.

questions.question: A tourist covers half of his journey by train at \(60\text{ km/h}\), half of the remainder by bus at \(30\text{ km/h}\) and the rest by cycle at \(10\text{ km/h}\). The average speed of the tourist in \(\text{km/h}\) during his entire journey is
questions.explanation:
Let the total distance of the journey be \(D\) km.
  • First segment (Train): Distance \(d_1 = \dfrac{D}{2}\), Speed \(v_1 = 60 \text{ km/h}\). \[\text{Time } t_1 = \frac{D/2}{60} = \frac{D}{120}\]
  • Second segment (Bus): Half of the remaining distance. Remaining distance \(= D - \dfrac{D}{2} = \dfrac{D}{2}\). \[d_2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{D}{2}\right) = \frac{D}{4}, \text{Speed} \, v_2 = 30 \text{ km/h}\] \[\text{Time } t_2 = \frac{D/4}{30} = \frac{D}{120}\]
  • Third segment (Cycle): The remaining portion. \(d_3 = D - \left(\dfrac{D}{2} + \dfrac{D}{4}\right) = \dfrac{D}{4}\), Speed \(v_3 = 10 \text{ km/h}\). \[\text{Time } t_3 = \frac{D/4}{10} = \frac{D}{40}\]
Average Speed Calculation: \[\text{Total Time } T = t_1 + t_2 + t_3 = \frac{D}{120} + \frac{D}{120} + \frac{D}{40} = \frac{D + D + 3D}{120} = \frac{5D}{120} = \frac{D}{24}\] \[\text{Average Speed} = \frac{\text{Total Distance}}{\text{Total Time}} = \frac{D}{D/24} = 24 \text{ km/h}\] \[\boxed{\text{C: 24}}\]
Key points
  • Average Speed: Never compute the simple arithmetic mean of the speeds (\(\dfrac{60+30+10}{3}\)). It must always be calculated as \(\dfrac{\text{Total Distance}}{\text{Total Time}}\).

questions.question: The current erection cost of a structure is \(Rs.\ 13,200\). If the labour wages per day increase by \(1/5\) of the current wages and the working hours decrease by \(1/24\) of the current period, then the new cost of erection in \(Rs.\) is
questions.explanation:
Let the initial parameters of construction costs be represented as: \[\text{Erection Cost } (C) \propto \text{Wages } (W) \times \text{Working Hours } (H) \implies C = k \cdot W \cdot H = 13,200\] Now, we apply the fractional scaling updates to each component:
  • New Wages (\(W'\)): Increases by \(\frac{1}{5} \implies W' = W\left(1 + \frac{1}{5}\right) = \frac{6}{5}W\)
  • New Working Hours (\(H'\)): Decreases by \(\frac{1}{24} \implies H' = H\left(1 - \frac{1}{24}\right) = \frac{23}{24}H\)
Formulating the new erection cost (\(C'\)): \[C' = k \cdot W' \cdot H' = k \cdot \left(\frac{6}{5}W\right) \cdot \left(\frac{23}{24}H\right)\] Extracting the proportional constants: \[C' = \left(\frac{6}{5} \times \frac{23}{24}\right) \cdot (k \cdot W \cdot H)\] \[C' = \left(\frac{1}{5} \times \frac{23}{4}\right) \cdot 13,200 = \frac{23}{20} \times 13,200\] \[C' = 23 \times 660 = 15,180\] \[\boxed{\text{B: 15,180 }}\]

questions.question: In the summer of 2012, in New Delhi, the mean temperature of Monday to Wednesday was 41\(^\circ\)C and of Tuesday to Thursday was 43\(^\circ\)C. If the temperature on Thursday was 15% higher than that of Monday, then the temperature in \(^\circ\)C on Thursday was
questions.explanation:
Let the temperatures of Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday be represented by \(M, T, W,\) and \(Th\) respectively. Step 1: Formulate sum equations from the averages
The mean temperature from Monday to Wednesday (3 days) was \(41^\circ\text{C}\): \[\frac{M + T + W}{3} = 41 \implies M + T + W = 123\] The mean temperature from Tuesday to Thursday (3 days) was \(43^\circ\text{C}\): \[\frac{T + W + Th}{3} = 43 \implies T + W + Th = 129\] Step 2: Find the relation between Thursday and Monday
Subtracting the first equation from the second: \[(T + W + Th) - (M + T + W) = 129 - 123 \implies Th - M = 6\] Step 3: Apply the percentage criteria
Thursday's temperature is given as \(15\%\) higher than Monday's: \[Th = 1.15M\] Substitute this back into the difference equation: \[1.15M - M = 6 \implies 0.15M = 6 \implies M = \frac{6}{0.15} = 40^\circ\text{C}\] Now compute Thursday's value: \[Th = M + 6 = 40 + 6 = 46^\circ\text{C}\] \[\boxed{\text{C: 46}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Always read the final line of the prompt to confirm which specific variable is requested. The question asks for Thursday (\(46^\circ\text{C}\)), not Monday (\(40^\circ\text{C}\)).

questions.question: A car travels 8 km in the first quarter of an hour, 6 km in the second quarter and 16 km in the third quarter. The average speed of the car in km per hour over the entire journey is
questions.explanation:
To calculate the net average speed, we evaluate the absolute total distance over the absolute total time consumed. Step 1: Compute Total Distance
\[\text{Total Distance} = 8 + 6 + 16 = 30\text{ km}\] Step 2: Compute Total Time
Each listed interval represents one quarter of an hour (\(\frac{1}{4}\) hour). Three intervals are traversed: \[\text{Total Time} = 3 \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{4}\text{ hour}\] Step 3: Evaluate Average Speed
\[\text{Average Speed} = \dfrac{\text{Total Distance}}{\text{Total Time}} = \dfrac{30}{\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)} = 30 \times \dfrac{4}{3} = 40\text{ km/h}\] \[\boxed{\text{C: 40}}\]
Key points
  • Average Speed Criteria: Average speed must strictly be solved as global distance divided by global time, avoiding basic arithmetic averages of localized speeds.

questions.question: Find the sum to \(n\) terms of the series \(10 + 84 + 734 + \dots\)
questions.explanation:
The terms of the series are: \(10, 84, 734, \dots\) We can break down each term relative to powers of 9:
  • \(T_1 = 10 = 9^1 + 1\)
  • \(T_2 = 84 = 9^2 + 3 = 81 + 3\)
  • \(T_3 = 734 = 9^3 + 5 = 729 + 5\)
Thus, the general term can be written as: \[T_r = 9^r + (2r - 1)\] Summing up to \(n\) terms (\(S_n\)):
\[S_n = \sum_{r=1}^{n} T_r = \sum_{r=1}^{n} 9^r + \sum_{r=1}^{n} (2r - 1)\] Evaluating the two independent parts:
  • The first component is a Geometric Progression (GP) with first term \(a=9\) and common ratio \(R=9\): \[\sum_{r=1}^{n} 9^r = \dfrac{9(9^n - 1)}{9 - 1} = \dfrac{9(9^n - 1)}{8}\]
  • The second component is the summation of the first \(n\) consecutive odd integers, which simplifies to: \[\sum_{r=1}^{n} (2r - 1) = n^2\]
Combining these components yields: \[S_n = \dfrac{9(9^n - 1)}{8} + n^2\] \[\boxed{\text{D: $\dfrac{9(9^n - 1)}{8} + n^2 $}}\]

questions.question: The set of values of \(p\) for which the roots of the equation \(3x^2 + 2x + p(p-1) = 0\) are of opposite sign is
questions.explanation:
Given the quadratic equation: \[3x^2 + 2x + p(p-1) = 0\] For a quadratic equation \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\) to possess roots of entirely **opposite signs**, the product of its roots (\(\alpha\beta\)) must be strictly negative. Using the relation \(\alpha\beta = \frac{c}{a}\): \[\alpha\beta = \dfrac{p(p-1)}{3} < 0\] Since the denominator is positive, this inequality matches: \[p(p-1) < 0\] The roots of the boundary are \(p=0\) and \(p=1\). Testing intervals via the sign-wave method confirms the product is negative when \(p\) lies strictly between these bounds: \[p \in (0, 1)\] \[\boxed{\text{B: (0, 1)}}\]
Key points
  • Roots of Opposite Signs: This criterion is fully satisfied if and only if \(\dfrac{c}{a} < 0\). When the product of the roots is strictly negative, real roots are guaranteed automatically (\(D > 0\)), making an independent discriminant calculation redundant.

questions.question: What is the chance that a leap year, selected at random, will contain 53 Saturdays?
questions.explanation:
A leap year comprises exactly \(366\) days. Converting this into complete weeks: \[366 \text{ days} = 52 \text{ weeks} \times 7 \text{ days/week} + 2 \text{ leftover days} = 364 \text{ days} + 2 \text{ leftover days}\] Every leap year naturally secures 52 Saturdays. To log exactly **53 Saturdays**, one of the 2 leftover days must hit a Saturday. The 2 leftover days form consecutive pairs. The complete set of equally likely configurations for these days is:
  1. Sunday and Monday
  2. Monday and Tuesday
  3. Tuesday and Wednesday
  4. Wednesday and Thursday
  5. Thursday and Friday
  6. Friday and Saturday
  7. Saturday and Sunday
Out of these 7 pairs, exactly 2 contain a Saturday (Friday-Saturday and Saturday-Sunday). Thus, the probability is: \[P(53 \text{ Saturdays}) = \dfrac{2}{7}\] \[\boxed{\text{A: 2/7 }}\]
Key points
  • Calendar Probability Structures: Non-leap years carry 1 leftover day (yielding a \(\frac{1}{7}\) probability for 53 identical days), whereas leap years feature 2 leftover days (yielding a \(\frac{2}{7}\) probability).
